extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel, and patent prosecutors evaluating §101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and distilled standards for evaluating U.S. patent claim eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (the Alice two-step framework), based on district court holdings and examples of abstract ideas and inventive-concept analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are evaluated for whether they are 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, mathematical formulas, or other concepts long prevalent in human activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly identifies claims as 'directed to the abstract idea of' with many examples: presenting iterations of products to entice business; responding to a sender of a message; controlling access by verifying credentials; granting access after payment; setting up/managing a cloud computing environment; communicating information about a mailpiece by marking; matching purchase data to households; filtering financial data into formats; address directories; forecasting demand; hedging risk; notifying customers of package status; collecting customer membership/discount information; suggesting ways around ATM limits; reference checking applicants; administering a test; preparing video for streaming; retrieving and arranging documents by frequency of use; using notebook-type tabs to label spreadsheets; multicasting and transmitting information; etc. If a claim's focus maps to one of these types of longstanding human practices or abstract concepts, courts have treated it as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea that is not computer- or network-specific remains abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed idea is not specifically tied to computer or network technology, courts treat it as abstract even if implemented on computers or networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: presenting product iterations was held 'not computer or network specific'; an address directory and many business methods were 'neither novel nor specific to interactive television systems' yet implemented on generic computers. Applying an abstract idea to the Internet or web-based applications does not alone make it non-abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept when claim elements are generic computer components
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims lack an inventive concept if they merely recite generic computer hardware or software to perform conventional steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cases hold that reciting a 'processor, memory device, and computing device,' or 'sending a message over the internet,' or 'generic computer components' does not supply an inventive concept. Courts reject claims that 'merely employ generic hardware and software' or do not place meaningful limitations on hardware or software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation via a generic computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Automating an abstract idea by implementing it on a generic computer does not make the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated holdings: 'mere automation through a generic computer' is insufficient; claims that simply 'automate[d] what a person could do manually with a general purpose computer' lack an inventive concept, even if more efficient or less error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims not tied to a particular machine or specific technical implementation lack inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is not tied to a particular machine or does not describe specific hardware/software techniques is more likely to lack an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts noted that inventions 'not tied to a particular machine' or that 'do not recite how' functions are performed 'in a manner that generates [technical] data' fail to provide an inventive concept. Attempts to imply specific hardware from the specification without explicit tying have been found insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing some steps not previously employed is not alone enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating that 'some of the steps were not previously employed in this art' does not, standing alone, confer patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that novelty of individual steps does not substitute for an inventive concept that meaningfully transforms an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-performable tasks or processes that can be done mentally indicate abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim describes tasks that humans could perform mentally or in the human realm, courts treat the claimed subject matter as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example holdings: digital matching processes that can be performed by humans confirmed abstractness; claims that 'can be performed by humans rather than computers' support finding an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying known concepts to web/Internet environments is insufficient without technical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating a conventional concept to a web-based or networked environment does not create an inventive concept absent specialized technology or improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holdings: applying verification to interactive television, performing known concepts 'to web-based software applications,' or implementing data labeling on the Internet were held insufficient because they merely used general purpose computers and did not disclose technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a mathematical formula or algorithm alone is not patentable without inventive application
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering a new mathematical algorithm or formula does not by itself support a patent unless there is some other inventive concept in its application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court example: a new mathematical formula for selecting colors was held insufficient absent an inventive application. The page emphasizes that mathematical discoveries must be applied in a way that adds an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed or efficiency improvements alone do not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that only increase speed, efficiency, or frequency of performing a known process—without an innovative method—do not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: software updates 'happen more frequently and quickly' via the Internet but that was not considered an inventive concept. Similarly, 'increasing speed, without some innovative method producing the increase, is not in itself an inventive step.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for specific technical description of how steps are performed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification/claim that explains how steps are technically performed or claims an improvement in the means of performing the steps supports eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts criticized patents that 'do not disclose any technical description of how the steps in the process take place' or 'do not recite any improvement to technology.' By contrast, claims that disclosed 'innovative technology' (e.g., using engine frequency to measure run time) or solved a technological flaw were treated as eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete, tangible instruments or physical components can transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to concrete physical devices or components that utilize specific techniques can be 'significantly more' than mere abstract concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: infusion pump battery gauge and medication level controller claims were held not to be abstract because they were 'concrete, tangible instrument[s]' using a sampling detection technique and provided dynamic automatic adjustment, which went beyond mere calculation or improved speed/efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that provide a technological improvement or solve a problem rooted in computer technology may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention addresses a technological problem and provides a concrete technological improvement (not merely a business or abstract solution), courts may find patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a judge found claims overcoming 'the inability to remotely install software on-demand without pre-installation' to supply inventive concept; claims that 'address specific problems and provided the necessary technological improvements' were held not directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely recite conventional activities like receipt, storage, processing, or data collection are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level recitations of receipt, storage, processing, gathering, labeling, and delivering data are treated as abstract and lacking inventive concept when implemented with generic technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several holdings labeled claims as abstract where they covered 'receipt, storage, and processing,' 'collecting and organizing information,' 'gathering and labeling information,' 'collecting delivery information,' 'sending and storing messages,' and similar conventional data-management activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that lack meaningful limitations on hardware/software are generic
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims do not meaningfully limit or specify hardware or software, they are treated as generic implementations and lack an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court language: 'no meaningful limitations are placed on any of the hardware or software' supports ineligibility. Bare recitals of commonplace components without specifics were repeatedly rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite a novel and ordered combination of existing elements to show inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere aggregation of known elements will not provide an inventive concept unless the elements are combined in a novel, non-routine, and meaningful way that imposes limitations beyond the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims 'did not recite a novel and ordered combination of existing elements' and were therefore held ineligible. Courts look for an inventive interplay or particular arrangement that yields a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits asserted in briefs but not recited in the claims do not support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are judged by their actual recitations, not by hypothetical or asserted benefits not included in claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a patentee's claim of large-scale tracking benefits or privacy advantages that were not recited in the claims were disregarded in the eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conventional third-party intermediaries or commonplace authentication techniques is abstract when implemented generically
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a third party or a random time-sensitive code for authentication is treated as an abstract concept if nothing in the claims renders the implementation unconventional or technological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example holdings described claims as 'using a third party and a random, time-sensitive code to confirm identity' and concluded lack of inventive concept because they were implemented with generic computer components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that enable routine business or organizational tasks simply by digitization are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting conventional business practices, organizational tasks, or administrative processes into a computerized form without inventive technological changes yields ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: membership discount programs, check financing systems, trucking manifests, and administering tests were held abstract when merely implemented on computers or networks with routine components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that describe novel technical measurement techniques or sensing tied to physical parameters may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovative uses of physical measurements or sensing (e.g., using engine frequency to measure run time, sampling detection techniques) that materially change how a device functions can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: remote monitoring of fleet vehicles using engine frequency and certain imaging/sensing claims were found to involve 'innovative technology' or concrete techniques that support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are premature to judge for inventive concept prior to claim construction or factual development
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances, courts decline to resolve inventive-concept issues at early stages (e.g., pre-claim-construction) because factual development may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes instances where courts sustained objections or found the inventive-concept determination premature, indicating eligibility analysis can depend on claim construction and factual record.
